title: EF Core Audit Trail - Two-Layer System
one_line_summary: A two-layer audit system combining entity-level BaseAuditableEntity stamps with separate operation log tables for both system and domain events.
executive_summary: This tutorial explains how to build a comprehensive audit trail in EF Core using two complementary layers: Layer 1 is a BaseAuditableEntity inheritance chain that stamps every record with CreatedAt/ModifiedAt/DeletedByUserId, and Layer 2 is a pair of log tables (AuditLog for system events like logins, CrmActivityLog for domain events like lead stage changes). It deliberately rejects EF Core interceptors in favor of manual field population in service code, trading DRY for explicitness and solving the userId access problem. The doc also covers soft deletes, append-only log design, and why you should audit writes but not reads.
suggested_metaphor: Think of this like a library book. Layer 1 is the stamp card glued inside the cover - a quick glance tells you who last checked it out and when. Layer 2 is the librarian's ledger at the front desk - a separate book recording every single event: who borrowed it, who returned it late, who spilled coffee on it. The stamp is fast to read but shallow; the ledger is richer but you have to flip through pages. A good library needs both.
suggested_intro_hook: A regulator walks in and asks: 'Show me exactly who changed this customer's address last Tuesday, and prove nobody tampered with the record afterward.' If your answer is 'let me grep the logs,' you've already lost. This is the architecture that makes that question a 30-second SQL query instead of a 3-day investigation.
what_it_teaches: How to architect a compliant, debuggable audit system for a multi-tenant ASP.NET Core + EF Core application. Covers the design tension between automatic (interceptor) and manual (service-layer) audit population, why GivingCare chose manual, how to split system vs domain audit storage across databases, and UI patterns for displaying audit timelines with MudBlazor.
key_takeaways: Use inheritance (BaseEntity -> BaseAuditableEntity -> BaseSoftDeletableEntity) to give entities audit fields for free
Manual audit population in services is more explicit and easier to debug than interceptors, at the cost of repetition
System-level audit (logins) belongs in a central DB; domain-level audit (business events) belongs per-tenant
Wrap audit log writes in try/catch so logging failures never break business operations
Audit logs must be append-only - never expose Update or Delete on your audit service
Always store UtcNow, never Now; local time belongs in the UI layer only
Don't audit reads - only audit state changes, or you'll drown in noise
quality_notes: Excellent tutorial. Well-structured with clear visual diagrams, code examples for both the chosen pattern and the alternative (interceptor) pattern, honest discussion of trade-offs, and concrete 'good vs poor audit entry' comparisons. Numbered 23 suggests part of a series.

title: ConcurrentDictionary and Thread-Safe Caching
one_line_summary: ConcurrentDictionary uses lock striping to let many threads read and write the same cache simultaneously, replacing fragile Dictionary+lock patterns with a one-line GetOrAdd call.
executive_summary: This tutorial explains why a plain Dictionary is lethal under concurrent access (internal bucket corruption, infinite FindEntry loops) and how ConcurrentDictionary solves it via per-segment lock striping. It walks through four real patterns from the codebase (compiled expression cache, MethodInfo cache, ChatHub online users with snapshot-on-lock, facial recognition callback router) and explicitly calls out two broken patterns - a Dictionary+manual double-checked lock and lock() guarding async initialization - showing why SemaphoreSlim(1,1) is the correct tool when await is involved.
suggested_metaphor: A regular Dictionary is a single-lane bridge - one car crosses at a time and two cars from opposite ends crash. A ConcurrentDictionary is a 16-lane highway where each lane has its own traffic light (on a 4-core machine, that's ProcessorCount * 4 stripes). Two cars going to different lanes don't even notice each other. And GetOrAdd is the drive-through: if your order is already in the system it hands you the bag; if not, the kitchen cooks it once and files the recipe - next customer asking for the same thing just grabs the bag.
suggested_intro_hook: Your Blazor Server app crashes at 3am with a NullReferenceException deep inside Dictionary.FindEntry. The stack trace is useless. You add logs. It happens again. The actual cause? Two threads adding to a static cache at the exact same nanosecond, corrupting the internal bucket chain. This is a bug you cannot fix with more logging - you can only fix it by using the right data structure.
what_it_teaches: How to pick the right concurrency primitive for shared state in Blazor Server (or any multi-threaded .NET app). When to use ConcurrentDictionary vs Dictionary+lock, when ConcurrentDictionary alone isn't enough (mutable values need their own lock), why lock() cannot guard async code, and what SemaphoreSlim(1,1) gives you that a monitor lock does not.
key_takeaways: Any static or shared Dictionary MUST be a ConcurrentDictionary - no exceptions
GetOrAdd replaces double-checked locking with one atomic line
The factory passed to GetOrAdd may run more than once under contention, but only one result is stored
ConcurrentDictionary makes the dictionary thread-safe, not its values - mutable values still need their own lock
Never hold a lock across an await - copy to a snapshot first, release the lock, then do async I/O
You cannot await inside a lock() block - use SemaphoreSlim(1,1).WaitAsync() instead
Lock striping means unrelated keys on different stripes never block each other
quality_notes: Excellent tutorial with multiple real-world examples from the actual codebase, including both correct and anti-pattern cases. Honest call-outs of broken patterns (GlobalChatService) make it unusually useful. Numbered 22 in the Education series.

title: EF Core Multi-Tenant Database Pattern
one_line_summary: A single DbContext class can serve many tenant databases by taking the database name as a constructor parameter and resolving the connection string dynamically in OnConfiguring.
executive_summary: This tutorial teaches the database-per-tenant pattern using ONE DynamicCompanyContext class whose OnConfiguring method resolves a different connection string based on a companyKey constructor parameter. It covers the full lifecycle: abstract BaseContext with shared DbSets, concrete DynamicCompanyContext, IDesignTimeDbContextFactory for CLI tooling, separate migration folders for auth vs tenant contexts, runtime tenant provisioning via MigrateAsync, and a reusable TenantMigrator utility wired into Program.cs with a --migrate-tenants CLI flag.
suggested_metaphor: Imagine a locksmith who makes one universal lock body but cuts different keys. The lock body (DynamicCompanyContext) is identical everywhere - same tumblers, same shape. The key (companyKey) is what determines which door it opens. You don't need a different locksmith for every building, and adding a new building just means cutting one more key. Your appsettings.json is the key-cutting template, and TenantMigrator.MigrateAllTenantsAsync is the locksmith going around to every door to make sure they all still fit after a security upgrade.
suggested_intro_hook: Your boss just sold the SaaS to its 50th customer and each one wants their data in a separate database for compliance. The naive approach would be 50 context classes - one per tenant. That way madness lies. Here's the pattern that turns 50 classes into 1 class and makes adding the 51st tenant a two-line config change.
what_it_teaches: How to build a multi-tenant SaaS with physical database isolation using EF Core, without duplicating context classes per tenant. Covers the runtime/design-time split (DI at runtime vs IDesignTimeDbContextFactory for CLI), why migrations need separate output folders per context, the danger of mixing EnsureCreatedAsync with MigrateAsync, and how to provision new tenants idempotently at runtime.
key_takeaways: One DbContext class can serve infinite tenants if you parameterize the connection string
The design-time factory is only for dotnet ef CLI tools - runtime uses DI
Use separate --output-dir folders for each context's migrations
MigrateAsync is idempotent - safe to run repeatedly on already-migrated databases
Never mix EnsureCreatedAsync and MigrateAsync on the same database
Adding a new tenant should be a config change, not a code change
Use modelBuilder.Ignore<T>() to prevent central-DB tables from leaking into tenant DBs via navigation properties
quality_notes: Excellent and complete tutorial. Covers both the concept and the operational details (CLI commands, appsettings structure, gotchas table). The 'from zero to multi-tenant' section provides a clear end-to-end narrative. Only minor gap: doesn't discuss row-level security as an alternative to database-per-tenant.

title: Sistema de Produção de Chão de Fábrica - Documentação Técnica (PT)
one_line_summary: Portuguese-language formal technical documentation of the FactoryFloor MES system covering architecture, components, services, transactions, and Primavera ERP integration.
executive_summary: A formal Portuguese-language technical reference for the BioBraga FactoryFloor manufacturing execution system (MES), a Blazor Server + MudBlazor + EF Core application that tracks production orders, material consumption, and stock movements in real time. It documents the three-layer architecture (Presentation/Service/Data), the Factory_New.razor page with its PIN-based worker authentication and machine filtering, the MaterialConsumptionModal with its 1.5-second debounced loading and multi-step transaction flow, and the FactoryFloorService with its transactional stock movement generation (ENTSTOCK/SAIDASTOCK/DESP documents). Also covers Primavera ERP integration, DbContextFactory connection pooling, and variance analysis DTOs.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Manufacturing plants need a real-time link between the physical shop floor and the ERP system. Workers on the floor must be able to start, pause, and finish production orders, record actual material consumption versus planned consumption, and have every action automatically generate the correct stock movements (entries, exits, waste documents) in Primavera ERP. Without this bridge, inventory drift occurs, compliance suffers, and managers cannot see what's actually being produced versus what's planned. The system exists to give BioBraga real-time visibility into production orders and to automate the accounting flow that feeds back into Primavera.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides a Blazor Server interface where authenticated workers (via hashed PIN) can select a machine, see the production orders assigned to it, start/pause/stop production, and submit material consumption data. The MaterialConsumptionModal dynamically loads the required materials proportional to the quantity produced, compares actual versus planned quantities with variance analysis, and displays historical consumption averages. On submission, a database transaction updates the order quantities, decrements material consumption tracking, generates three kinds of stock documents (ENTSTOCK for finished goods, SAIDASTOCK for materials consumed, DESP for waste), and forwards the movements to the Primavera ERP via a repository abstraction.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The architecture follows a strict Presentation -> Service -> Data flow. Factory_New.razor is the main page, accepting an optional maquinaid route parameter for machine-specific views; it uses CascadingParameter for the current worker and filters orders locally to avoid server roundtrips. MaterialConsumptionModal uses a CancellationTokenSource-based debounce (1.5 seconds) on the QuantityProduced input to avoid thrashing when workers type values. FactoryFloorService is scoped in DI and receives an IDbContextFactory<BioBragaContext>, an IPrimaveraRepository, and an ILogger. The core transaction in RegisterProductionAsync wraps everything in a BeginTransactionAsync: update order quantities, update gastoFase consumption tracking, generate stock movements via GenerateStockEntryAsync/GenerateStockExitAsync, and CommitAsync - with rollback on any exception. Material calculation uses a simple proportional formula (totalPlannedForOrder / orderQuantity * quantityProduced), optionally using QuantidadeMedia historical averages when present. Context reuse is done via a 'shouldDisposeContext' pattern so nested service calls can share one transaction. Security uses Utils.Hash(pin) for PIN validation and filters by worker.Isactive, with all actions logged to CrmOrdemProducaoLog with a Criadopor field for audit.

suggested_metaphor: Think of this system as a real-time cashier for a factory kitchen. The worker is the chef, the machine is their station, the production order is a recipe card taped to the counter. When the chef finishes a batch, they punch in their PIN (hashed, like a bank card), say 'I made 47 units using 2.3kg of sugar instead of the planned 2.5kg,' and the cashier - FactoryFloorService - simultaneously marks the recipe done, updates the sugar jar level, prints three receipts (one for finished food, one for sugar used, one for the spilled sugar), and faxes a copy to the accountant at Primavera ERP. If anything goes wrong mid-receipt, the transaction rolls back and nothing is half-done.
suggested_intro_hook: How do you build a factory-floor interface that survives a worker slamming the Enter key ten times, a tablet with patchy wifi, a manager demanding historical variance analysis, and an ERP system that needs every material movement properly documented - all while running transactionally so a crash mid-save never leaves stock half-decremented?
what_it_teaches: How to architect a real-world manufacturing execution system in Blazor Server that bridges a local operations database with an external ERP via repositories, uses database transactions to keep stock and production order state consistent, implements PIN-based worker authentication with hashed credentials, and handles UX concerns like debounced inputs and multi-step progress feedback.
key_takeaways: Use IDbContextFactory<T> for connection pooling in long-lived Blazor Server circuits
Wrap multi-step business operations in BeginTransactionAsync for atomicity
Debounce input-driven async loads with CancellationTokenSource
Filter collections client-side when possible to avoid server roundtrips
Use the Repository pattern to abstract external ERP integration from business logic
Hash PINs before storage, never compare plaintext
Pass a 'shouldDisposeContext' flag when sharing a DbContext across nested service calls
quality_notes: Well-structured formal reference document in Portuguese. Covers the full stack from UI components down to transaction handling and deployment config. Mirrors the English FactoryFloor documentation - treat as the PT counterpart of factory-floor-system domain. Some ASCII diagrams lost alignment in PDF extraction.

title: Generic Schedule Grid Architecture
one_line_summary: A reusable Blazor component that schedules any entity type (employees, equipment, jobs) through a generic IScheduleGridDataProvider<TSchedule> abstraction with pluggable per-entity providers.
executive_summary: An architectural walkthrough of the GenericScheduleGrid<TSchedule> Blazor component, which uses the Strategy pattern (via IScheduleGridDataProvider<TSchedule>) to support scheduling across employees, equipment, and jobs without duplicating grid UI code. Each entity type gets its own data provider (JobEmployeeScheduleDataProvider, EmployeeJobScheduleDataProvider, etc.) registered in DI and paired with a thin wrapper component. Schedules implement IScheduleEntry for uniform overlap detection, and the grid switches between JobCentric and EntityCentric view modes. The doc explains the folder structure, DI registration, integration into Jobs.razor and detail pages, and a step-by-step guide for adding a new entity type.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The application has three different 'things' that get scheduled: employees (who works when), equipment (what's in use when), and jobs (what tasks are happening). Without a shared component, each would need its own grid UI, its own CRUD logic, and its own conflict detection - three parallel implementations drifting apart over time. The GenericScheduleGrid exists so that UI polish (drag to create, click to edit, color-coded cells) only has to be written once, while each entity type plugs in its own data loading and persistence logic behind a clean interface.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Renders a reusable time-grid UI where rows are entities (employees, equipment, or jobs depending on context) and cells are schedule entries. Supports two fundamental viewing modes: JobCentric (fixed axis is a job, rows are people/equipment working on it) used in the Jobs page, and EntityCentric (fixed axis is a person/equipment, rows are jobs they're assigned to) used in detail pages. It handles create, update, delete, batch operations, cross-midnight shift detection, overlap detection, and context title/info lookups - all delegating the actual data access to a provider injected per usage.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The grid is a single Blazor component GenericScheduleGrid<TSchedule> where TSchedule : IScheduleEntry, parameterized with ContextId, DataProvider, CompanyDatabase, and UserId. The provider implements IScheduleGridDataProvider<TSchedule> and exposes GetRowsAsync, GetSchedulesAsync, CreateScheduleAsync, UpdateScheduleAsync, DeleteScheduleAsync, CreateNewSchedule, and CloneSchedule. Four concrete providers exist: JobEmployeeScheduleDataProvider, JobEquipmentScheduleDataProvider, EmployeeJobScheduleDataProvider, EquipmentJobScheduleDataProvider - each registered scoped in Program.cs and wrapped by a tiny .razor file (JobEmployeeScheduleTab, EmployeeScheduleTab, EquipmentScheduleTab) that injects the right provider and forwards parameters. The schedule entities (JobSchedule, JobEquipmentSchedule) all implement IScheduleEntry so the grid can call OverlapsWith and CalculatedTotalHours without caring about the concrete type. Adding a fifth entity type (vehicles) is a checklist: create a schedule model, a data provider, optionally a conflict strategy, register in DI, create a wrapper component, drop it into the relevant detail page.

suggested_metaphor: The GenericScheduleGrid is a universal remote control. The remote itself (the grid UI with its buttons and screen) never changes - you can use it with your TV, your stereo, or your air conditioner. What changes is which 'device profile' (data provider) you load into it. The profile knows which commands map to which hardware quirks. Adding a new gadget doesn't mean buying a new remote - it just means writing a new profile and plugging it in. And because every device must respond to basic commands like Power and Volume (the IScheduleEntry interface), the remote can always show a sensible default UI no matter what you plug in.
suggested_intro_hook: You just finished writing a beautiful employee scheduling grid. Now your boss says 'make equipment work the same way.' Then 'now jobs.' Then 'now vehicles.' You can copy the grid three more times and pray the bugs stay in sync, or you can do what this architecture does: write the grid once, write the data loading four times, and let the compiler prove every entity type obeys the same rules.
what_it_teaches: How to apply the Strategy pattern to Blazor components using generics and interfaces so that a single component can serve multiple entity types without compromising type safety. Also demonstrates IoC-based provider selection via wrapper components, the difference between JobCentric and EntityCentric view modes, and how SOLID principles map onto a practical scheduling problem (OCP via new providers, LSP via IScheduleEntry, DIP via interface-based grid dependency).
key_takeaways: Use a generic component with a provider interface to support N entity types with one UI
Concrete providers encapsulate entity-specific data access behind a common contract
Thin wrapper .razor files inject the right provider so pages don't know the grid is generic
IScheduleEntry as a uniform contract enables polymorphic overlap and hours calculations
JobCentric vs EntityCentric modes let the same grid answer 'who is on this job?' and 'where is this person scheduled?'
Adding a new entity type is a 6-step checklist: model, provider, strategy, DI, wrapper, integration
SOLID principles naturally fall out of this design: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP all apply
quality_notes: Excellent architectural doc. Clean diagrams, full interface listings, concrete provider examples, DI registration, and a step-by-step 'add a new entity type' recipe. The SOLID and Design Patterns tables at the end tie the implementation to theory nicely.

title: IdentityLearning Project Knowledge Base
one_line_summary: A complete onboarding knowledge base for the IdentityLearning Blazor Server app, covering architecture, setup, Identity features, email integration, security, deployment, and troubleshooting.
executive_summary: A comprehensive project knowledge base for the IdentityLearning project - an ASP.NET Core 9.0 Blazor Server app built to demonstrate enterprise Identity features (2FA with QR codes, email confirmation, password reset, account lockout, custom ApplicationUser with Department/IsActive/ColaboratorId). Documents the solution structure, MudBlazor 8 UI integration, a SOAP-based AgileEmailService, user secrets setup, EF Core migrations, role management configuration, password policy, security headers, and deployment strategies (IIS, Azure CLI). Includes troubleshooting for common issues and a quick-start checklist.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The developer needed a production-grade reference Identity implementation they could both learn from and use as a scaffold for real apps. Most online Identity tutorials stop at 'user can register' - this project goes further into real-world requirements: 2FA enrollment with QR codes, email confirmation flow, password reset, account lockout after failed attempts, custom user properties, and a SOAP email service integration specific to the Agile ecosystem. It doubles as a knowledge base so any new developer on the team can clone, run, and extend without having to figure out the conventions from scratch.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides a complete Blazor Server Identity application with registration, login, logout, email confirmation, password reset, two-factor authentication (TOTP with QR code generator), account lockout, and a profile management area. The custom ApplicationUser extends IdentityUser with Department, IsActive, and ColaboratorId for integration with the Agile employee domain. Emails are sent via a SOAP-based AgileEmailService that supports templated HTML emails and table markup ([TABLE:name]...[/TABLE] blocks). Configuration is externalized into appsettings plus User Secrets for sensitive values, and the database is managed via EF Core migrations.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The Program.cs wires up Identity with AddIdentityCore<ApplicationUser>().AddRoles<IdentityRole>().AddEntityFrameworkStores<ApplicationDbContext>(), configures password policy (min 8 chars, digit/upper/lower/non-alphanumeric required), and account lockout (5 attempts, 5 minute cooldown). The Components/Account folder holds Razor pages for all Identity flows - Pages/ for Login/Register/Manage, Shared/ for common components, .cs files for services and helpers. MudStaticTextField is used throughout for SSR compatibility. AgileEmailService implements an SOAP client that posts to https://axrm.agileincloud.com/agMailService/agEmailService.asmx using a service key stored in User Secrets, and emails can include a custom [TABLE:name] markup that is converted to HTML tables server-side. Migrations are added with dotnet ef migrations add and applied with dotnet ef database update, and the deployment story covers IIS (no-managed-code app pool), Azure (az webapp up), and environment variables for secrets in production.

suggested_metaphor: This project is like the IKEA manual for your authentication system. It doesn't just say 'put screws in holes' - it tells you which screwdriver to use, which holes are optional, where to find the allen keys (User Secrets), what to do if a shelf is wobbly (troubleshooting), and how to assemble the whole thing on different surfaces (IIS, Azure, local). By the time you're done, you don't just have a functioning wardrobe, you understand why each piece is there.
suggested_intro_hook: ASP.NET Core Identity gives you 80% of what you need for authentication - until someone asks 'does it support 2FA with QR codes?' and 'can the emails include HTML tables?' and 'where do I store the SMTP password?' This project is the 20% that turns a tutorial into a shippable app.
what_it_teaches: How to assemble a production-grade ASP.NET Core Identity application: extending IdentityUser with custom properties, configuring password and lockout policies, wiring up 2FA with QR codes, integrating an external SOAP email service, using User Secrets for sensitive configuration, structuring Identity pages for Blazor SSR, and deploying to IIS or Azure.
key_takeaways: Extend IdentityUser by creating ApplicationUser with your custom properties and registering it in AddIdentityCore<ApplicationUser>
Use MudStaticTextField for SSR-compatible forms in Blazor Server Identity pages
Store all sensitive config (SMTP passwords, service keys) in User Secrets during dev and environment variables in prod
Password policy and lockout are configured inside AddIdentityCore options
.AddRoles<IdentityRole>() must be chained after AddIdentityCore to enable role management
SOAP email integration needs its own service abstraction rather than stuffing logic into controllers
Deploy IIS sites with 'No Managed Code' app pools for .NET Core apps
quality_notes: Comprehensive project knowledge base in reference-manual style. Good breadth across setup, config, features, security, testing, deployment, monitoring, and maintenance. Feels like project onboarding documentation rather than a focused tutorial. Timestamped August 2024, version 1.3.0.

title: EF Core Relationships, Lazy Loading and Virtual Properties
one_line_summary: A quick reference showing when to use lazy, eager, and explicit loading in EF Core, when the virtual keyword is actually needed, and why lazy loading is usually the wrong choice.
executive_summary: A concise EF Core cheat sheet covering navigation properties versus foreign keys, the three loading strategies (lazy/eager/explicit), the specific role of the virtual keyword (only required when lazy loading is enabled), the correct use of [NotMapped] for computed properties, and performance tips like using .Include() and .Select() to avoid N+1 queries. Includes a quick decision guide table for choosing the right approach per scenario.
suggested_metaphor: Think of EF Core's loading strategies as three different ways to order at a restaurant. Eager loading is a prix-fixe menu: you ask for the steak and it arrives with the vegetables, potatoes, and sauce all on one plate, one trip from the kitchen. Lazy loading is tapas: you get the steak, then when you reach for a potato the waiter runs back to the kitchen, then for a carrot another trip - by the end of your meal the waiter has done fifty laps (that's N+1). Explicit loading is when you flag the waiter down yourself and say 'now bring me the dessert' - controlled but manual. The virtual keyword is the little bell on your table that lets the waiter run off to the kitchen when you touch a side dish; without it, you can't do lazy loading at all.
suggested_intro_hook: Your page that lists 100 companies takes 4 seconds to load. You check the SQL log: 101 queries. One to fetch the companies, then 100 more - one per company - to fetch each country. That's lazy loading biting you. The fix is usually one line, and this doc tells you which line.
what_it_teaches: How EF Core loads related entities, the trade-offs of each strategy, when you actually need the virtual keyword (rarely), and how to avoid the N+1 query problem. Also clarifies when [NotMapped] is correct (computed properties) versus wrong (real navigation properties).
key_takeaways: Keep both the FK property (CountryId) and the navigation property (Country) on your entity
Use .Include() or .Select() instead of lazy loading for predictable performance
The virtual keyword is only needed when lazy loading is enabled - otherwise it's noise
Never put [NotMapped] on a real navigation property - it's for computed in-memory values only
Most production apps turn off lazy loading globally for predictability
Use .Select() to project only the columns you need and reduce wire traffic
.Include() generates a single JOIN; lazy loading generates N+1 queries
quality_notes: Compact, useful cheat sheet. Includes tables, decision guides, and code examples. Short (~680 words) but focused. Would pair well with a deeper doc on query optimization and change tracking.

title: Exemplo Cores - CSS Color System Example
one_line_summary: A self-contained HTML/CSS demo showing a full web color system using CSS custom properties (primary, secondary, neutrals, feedback colors) with hover states and feedback boxes.
executive_summary: A single-file HTML demo that establishes a reusable CSS design token system via :root custom properties. It defines primary (red #df2e26), secondary (orange #f26d28), neutrals, feedback colors (success green, error red, warning orange, info blue), links, and spacing variables - then applies them to a complete page layout (header, sidebar, main grid, footer) with buttons, feedback boxes, and links demonstrating hover states. Useful as a visual reference for a brand color system implemented purely with CSS variables.
suggested_metaphor: This file is like a paint chip booklet from a hardware store, except it's also showing you how the paint looks on a fake wall. All the colors are declared in one place at the top (the :root section), given names like --color-primary and --success, and then referenced everywhere else with var(). Change the hex in one place and the entire page repaints - like swapping out the master tin and every wall in the house updating simultaneously.
suggested_intro_hook: Your designer hands you a Figma file with nineteen shades of red and says 'the primary button should use red #3 but if it's in a warning box use red #5 with 10% transparency.' You can hard-code those hex values across 47 files and pray nothing drifts - or you can define them once as CSS variables and never touch a hex again.
what_it_teaches: How to build a small but complete CSS design system using custom properties: naming a color palette via :root, using var() for reuse, applying it to layout (grid-template-areas), feedback boxes, buttons with hover, and links. Also demonstrates using rgba() with fixed colors for subtle backgrounds and solid colors for borders.
key_takeaways: Define all reusable values (colors, spacing) as CSS custom properties in :root
Use var(--name) everywhere instead of hard-coded values for consistent theming
Hover variants are often a darker shade of the base color - define both
grid-template-areas is a clean way to define page layouts declaratively
Feedback states (success/error/warning/info) each get their own semantic name
Using rgba() of a named color for backgrounds gives subtle tints that still match the palette
quality_notes: Small live demo file (~320 lines, mostly inline CSS). It's a working example, not a narrative tutorial - no commentary, just code you can open in a browser. Useful as a reference template when starting a new UI. Portuguese labels in the DOM.
